title: The Tiger Moth: the engine per the references, then the in-line's cowl round it
html:
The engine first. The DH.82 reference match (REF_MATCH, the Sketchfab DH82 model) puts the propeller's line where engY 0.21 has it. The Gipsy is inverted (cylinders down), and the drawn engine is 0.705 m tall against the real Gipsy Major's 0.752 m (All-Aero: 1227 × 508 × 752 mm, about 136 kg dry). So it stays where it is. The 8 cm lower engine of the last draft is withdrawn: it departs from the reference.

Then the cowl. Today's spinner stood over the cowl's ring because the cowl never read engY: the rule folds it into the cowl's axis (nothing flown moves). The front is built round the engine's own box, from the in-line pod's tall, boxy section, and sized to what the drawing carries over its front half. One thing does not fit the real bonnet: our engine generator draws an inverted in-line's induction on top (entry G164), up to 0.34 m over the shaft where the type's bonnet runs 0.13-0.27 m. The cowl covers it with one blister near the firewall (the reference model's bonnet has a blister too). The real fix for that hump is in the engine drawing (the induction placeable at the side), which REF_MATCH already asked for.

title: The crease: which of the plane's rows make a nose boxy
html:
A study on 15 builds (crease_study.js; evidence crease_study.txt). The firewall's outline was fitted with the cowl's own section law, and the mismatch measured as the RMS of the half-width:

  • waist tied to the plane's waistline (waistY): 5-65 mm
  • waist free: 4-37 mm
  • free, plus the width at the top and bottom lines (wAftTop / wAftBot): 2-23 mm

What makes the boxy ones hard is not topRound / botRound on their own. It is the sill crease (crSill ≥ 2: Cub, C172, Mosquito-alike), which keeps the flanks full up to the waistline and puts a deck narrower than the flanks on top. The C172's firewall is two-tiered: 0.97 of its width under the sill, 0.77 above, a step no two-half section can follow. Round-topped cabins (topRound 1: E-811 card, Camel, Stearman, B-ITES) fit within 2-5 mm once the deck width is free.

What the rule does now: the waist on the plane's waistline (your rule) where the cabin is flat-sided, fitted where it is round-topped, and the roundness above and below fitted to the firewall. What would close the rest: the deck and keel widths (wAftTop / wAftBot, CABIN-CRAFT's rows). But the flight model reads them (the cowl's wetted area and its mass), so I have not used them without A0's word.

tag: Point 3 and point 7 · what poked through
title: Pods sized to the drawn engine, full section to the spinner, the propeller a little forward
html: The pods were sized to the engine's envelope, and the drawn engine is bigger: the O-320's top hardware by 6 cm, the Rotax 915's by 13 cm (the poking at the top). A pod now takes the drawn engine's top and sides between its back and the flange (exhaust stubs may still leave underneath, as on real nacelles). It holds its full section all the way to the spinner and closes in front of it: the propeller moves forward by the lip (4-12 cm), and the engine layer's shaft bridges the gap. Flown numbers identical.

title: A helmet over each cylinder, where the drawn engine puts them
html: The cheeks row now takes 3 to 14: one bump per cylinder of a radial, evenly round from the first one's azimuth (1 and 2 are the cheeks they always were, to the bit). The study tool reads the drawn engine: its heads (the vertices at the engine's own enclosing radius), their count, their phase round the crank and their station along the cowl. The barrel is cut to 0.84 of the heads' radius, and each helmet stands 12 mm over its head. On a nose the radial's front is round, the engine's size, to the row's 1.15 × the firewall and no further (this generated nose is smaller than its W-670: noted).

strips.title: Radial on a nose (a generated W-670 card)

title: The motor's pod stays tight; its mount plate follows
html: What poked out behind the electric pod was the engine's own mounting plate and the mount's spread (±0.31 m), drawn on the nacelle at a fixed 0.20 m whatever the motor. A cowled pod now hands the nacelle its own size (_cage_cowl.js podPlate), so the plate and the mount shrink to the pod. Every other cowl and every cowl-less engine keeps the plate it had. The turboprop is unchanged (the PT6's exhaust stacks pierce its skin, as on a real one).

title: Where the nose without an aero nose came from
html: It was my study plane, not the game: I set the engine mount by hand to over-the-wing on a generated nose-engine card, so its nose kept the empty engine nose. In the game, the Engine mount tile's Over the wing writes the aero nose (_cage_design.js NOSE_AERO: a 0.95 nose of four rings, its tip 0.98, drooped 0.10), and so does the new-plane chooser, which goes through that tile. The plane below is rebuilt with the tile's own values.

title: A pusher narrows toward its engine
html: Your busher's front is 0.62 of its aft face's width; the rule now narrows a pusher and an in-line toward the engine too (the engine's half-width + 3 cm, never under 0.45 of the face). The busher's propeller line is also its engine's (engY 0.26, the Pusher tile's "engine top = boom bottom" rule), so its front is centred up there.
